Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

1 · Make it rough, make it early

A rough prototype is a question in material form. Make the smallest version that can teach you something.

A rough thing can answer a question that a polished thing hides.

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: Early-1900s photograph of Gaudí's hanging model for the Colonia Güell church: strings loaded with small sacks of weight hang from the ceiling, with paper draped over them to show the inverted form.

Maqueta polifunicular · Unknown photographer (Gaudí workshop, c. 1908) · Public domain · Source

  • A rough prototype is a question in material form.
  • It does not need to look finished. It needs to reveal one thing you do not know yet.
  • Build the smallest version that lets a classmate react.
  • "The prototype is meant to answer questions, so keep it focused."

Source: the prototype quote is (Knapp, Zeratsky, and Kowitz 2016, chap. 13); the lesson also cites (Cross 2006, vi) for design ability as resolving ill-defined problems. Other bullets and the slide's Tao line are course wording.

Ask: What can this rough object tell you that a description cannot?

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

2 · Defer judgement

Protect a short space for variation before you decide what works. Then judge with a named criterion.

Image: A page from Beethoven's 1812 sketchbook: hurried ink notation across many staves as themes for the Seventh Symphony are tried out.

Sketches for the second movement of Symphony no. 7, op. 92 (Petter Sketchbook, 1812) · Ludwig van Beethoven (sketchbook); Daderot (photograph, public-domain dedication) · Public domain · Source

  • Early critique can close a path before it shows what it might become.
  • Protect a short space for variation first. Then judge with a named criterion.
  • This is not permission to keep every idea. It stops you mistaking the first awkward version for the final limit.
  • Osborn's first rule: criticism is withheld until all ideas are in. In an experiment, college students who expected their artworks to be evaluated produced work judged less creative.

Source: the rule is (Osborn 1942, chap. 4); the evaluation result is (Amabile 1979, 221). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Which idea did you drop too early this week?

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

3 · Iterate with an exit

Write the test before the next version. Stop when the test is answered.

Course diagram · Koch triangle · #5cc4358a9bdb · Original course SVG

  • Revision helps when you know what the next version must answer.
  • Write one test before you change the work: "Can the viewer find the main action?" or "Does the form fit the brief?"
  • Stop when the test is answered, even if another improvement is possible.
  • Iteration can improve an idea, but it can also cause fixation: refining one option without considering others.

Source: the iteration/fixation bullet is (Dow et al. 2010, 18:1). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: What is the one test your next version must pass?

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

4 · Sketch to think

Three quick arrangements can show relationships that one polished drawing hides.

Sketching enables exploration of the problem space and the solution space to proceed together.

(Cross 2006, 37)

Course diagram · Koch triangle · #5cc4358a9bdb · Original course SVG

  • Draw three different arrangements, not one beautiful drawing.
  • Cross: "Sketching enables exploration of the problem space and the solution space to proceed together."
  • Compare relationships, rhythm and emphasis. A sketch is a temporary argument: it shows what your idea is doing.

Source: the quote is (Cross 2006, 37). The first and third bullets are course wording.

Ask: What did the second and third arrangement show that the first one hid?

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

5 · Open the solution space

Reframe an unclear brief as two or three questions. Make one small response to each.

(Beghetto and Karwowski 2025, 3)

Image: A spread from Paul Klee's 1925 Pedagogical Sketchbook: simple lines and shapes worked out as a 'first case', 'second case' and 'third case', each a different development.

Pädagogisches Skizzenbuch · Paul Klee · Public domain · Source

  • Some briefs are unclear because the problem itself is still moving. Do not force one path too soon.
  • Reframe the brief as two or three possible questions. Make one small response to each.
  • Creative agency: "the intentional and self-directed capacity to envision and enact new and meaningful actions within the existing constraints of a particular context".
  • Every way of stating a wicked problem already points to a solution.

Source: the wicked-problem bullet is (Buchanan 1992, 16); the creative-agency definition is (Beghetto and Karwowski 2025, 3). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Which of your questions surprised you most?

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

6 · Reflect at checkpoints

Write what changed, what stayed, and what the change taught you.

Image: Two pages of Orville Wright's diary for 17 December 1903: dense handwriting on squared notebook paper recording that day's series of flight tests.

Wright diary · Orville Wright · Public domain · Source

  • Pause after each version. Write three lines: what changed, what stayed, what the change taught you.
  • Schön: the situation "talks back", and in good design this conversation with the situation is reflective.
  • The checkpoint turns attempts into evidence you can discuss. It is a teaching prompt, not a model of every studio decision.

Source: the Schön bullet is (Schön 1983, 79). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: What did your last checkpoint teach you?

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

Exercise 1 · Same problem, three entry points, in parallel

Keep one D1 problem. Make three rough versions, each from a different starting point, before anyone gives feedback. Then show all three side by side.

Practises Masterclass 1, 3 and 4: rough and early, avoid fixation, sketch to think.

Save the problem, the three entry points, three scans and one sentence per version on what it taught you.

Image: An early-19th-century watercolour design sheet showing three chairs side by side, each with a differently curved back and patterned seat.

Design for Three Chairs with Curved Backs · Anonymous designer (early 19th century); The Metropolitan Museum of Art (CC0) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Timer: 20 minutes — about 15 making, 5 for side-by-side feedback in pairs.
  • One concrete D1 problem, the same for the whole class. Name three entry points before starting: structure, material/support, or audience/circulation.
  • Three rough sketches or small prototypes, one per entry point. Do not polish. No feedback until all three exist.
  • Show the three side by side; note what each taught you and which one the feedback favoured; mark ideas to combine.
  • Watch the temptation to solve it the obvious way and paste the entry point on afterwards.

Source: making several prototypes before feedback (parallel) gave novice designers better-performing and more varied designs, and a larger increase in task-specific self-confidence, than critique after each single prototype (Dow et al. 2010, 18:1); "a different entry point will usually mean a different train of ideas" is (de Bono 1970, chap. “Choice of Entry Point and Attention Area”). The steps and the watch-out are course wording.

Ask (in pairs): How did each entry point steer the path?

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

Exercise 2 · Delay judgement, then checkpoint and exit

Pick one version. Hold back judgement for five minutes, decide what it tests — role, look and feel, or how it works — revise once, and stop when your question is answered.

Practises Masterclass 2, 3 and 6: defer judgement, iterate with an exit, reflect at checkpoints.

Save before/after, the test question, the checkpoint lines and the exit decision.

Image: The Wright brothers' 1900 glider flying unmanned as a tethered kite against a cloudy sky, its two wings and struts clearly visible.

Wright Glider being flown as a kite, 1900 · Wilbur and Orville Wright · Public domain · Source

  • Timer: 20 minutes — about 5 delay, 5 question, 7 revise and test, 3 checkpoint.
  • Choose one of the three versions. For 5 minutes keep developing it without deciding whether it is right: no criticism, including your own.
  • Ask what this version tests: its role (what it does for the person), its look and feel, or how it would actually work. Pick one.
  • Write one testable question about that choice. Revise once; let a classmate try it.
  • Checkpoint: three lines — what changed, what stayed, what you learned. Exit when the question is answered, even if another improvement is possible.
  • If a tool or generative system supplied a variation, record the prompt, the option you rejected and why you kept the final form.

Source: withholding criticism "until all ideas are in" is Osborn's first ground rule (Osborn 1942, chap. 4). The role / look and feel / implementation question and the other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Where did you stop, and was it hard to stop?
